items.text: SEASON 12 · EPISODE 5 · DRAFT · CASE-064  Fenwright Group · month six — halfway · Maya, Rashida (CIO), Galen, Noor and Pim · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  Six months in, the rooms work better than they did. Rashida asks the question the contract was written around — and Maya answers it the only honest way: by counting, and putting her own name on the list.  ⚑ RV-187: succession is the CIO's to require. RV-189: people are credited, not blamed; nothing here is HR advice. RV-188: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: What Survives You
items.stakes: Halfway through the year: if the architect left tomorrow, what would break?
items.clock: The CIO wants a number by Friday.
items.reward: Every critical task with two people, every key decision with its reason — and a week to prove it.

items.prompt: How do you answer ‘what would break if you left?’
items.risk: An estate that works only while you're in it.
timeout: The question comes back in month eleven, with no time left.

hints.text: What would you count — and would you put your own name on it?

options.label: List every critical task and, for each, count who can do it unaided today — including yourself; and for each key decision, find where its reason is written
options.result: By Wednesday there are twenty-four tasks on the list. Eleven have one name next to them.
options.consequence: A number the CIO can watch.

options.label: Promise to stay reachable after you leave
options.result: Rashida: “Then I've hired an architect and bought a dependency.”

options.label: Write one big document of everything you know
options.result: Two hundred pages nobody has ever used.
options.consequence: Knowledge written is not knowledge held.

items.title: Eleven of twenty-four.
items.body: Twenty-four critical tasks; for each, who can do it unaided. Thirteen have two people or more. Eleven — 46% — have one. Seven only Galen can do: the platform restore, the service-account rotation, the booking link, a codec swap, the platform upgrade, re-imaging a room PC, vendor escalation. Four only Maya can do: rebuilding a DSP template, tuning a glass room, staging firmware, writing the lifecycle report. The architect hired to leave is on her own list.
items.label: Test: Galen's share — and what's left after Maya hands off.

items.alt: A grid of the 24 critical tasks, each marked with who can do it unaided: eleven highlighted red — seven ‘Galen only’, four ‘Maya only’; the rest ‘2+’. 11 of 24 (46%) with one person, and 0 of 14 key decisions with a written reason.
items.caption: Four of them are hers.

items.title: ‘re: glass rooms — gate the ceiling mics’
items.body: An email thread from month two: Maya to Teodor, ‘The echo in the glass rooms comes back through the ceiling mics when nobody's talking — gating them fixes it.’ The only place the reason existed.

items.prompt: Eleven single-person tasks, seven of them Galen's. How does coverage grow?
items.risk: An expert who feels replaced — or a list that never shrinks.
timeout: Galen restores the platform alone again at Christmas.

hints.text: How is a second person proven — and how does the expert feel about it?

options.label: Hire another senior technician
options.result: Six months to recruit. The new senior learns from Galen — slowly.
options.consequence: Money for a problem that's about teaching.

options.label: Pair every single-person task with a named second person, trained and signed off by doing it; Galen teaches his seven, credited as the expert; Maya hands off her four first
options.result: Noor takes the restore and the rotation, Pim the template rebuild. Maya's four are handed off by month seven.
options.consequence: Pairs, proven by doing — the expert credited, the architect first.

options.label: Ask Galen to write down everything he knows
options.result: Galen writes for a week and hates it. Nobody reads it.

options.label: Automate the seven tasks
options.result: Three can be. Four need judgment.

items.title: The fire nobody could remake
items.body: For centuries the Byzantine Empire defended itself with ‘Greek fire’, a burning liquid sprayed from ships that water couldn't put out. Its recipe was a state secret, known to very few people and never written where outsiders might read it. It worked — until the few people who knew were gone. The recipe was lost, and historians still argue over what it was. A secret known by a handful of people isn't protected. It's endangered.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #116 · AVERY'S LENS  Count who can do it — and write down why  An estate survives its people when every critical task can be done by at least two of them, and every key decision carries its reason with it.  Eleven of twenty-four critical tasks could be done by one person — four of them by the architect hired to leave.
Act II — “Why is it like this?”

items.title: Why is it like this?
items.body: Thursday afternoon Noor, tidying the glass-room DSP template, flags the ceiling-mic gating as redundant — ‘the mics are already muted when nobody's talking, aren't they?’ They aren't. In month two Maya found that in the eighteen glass rooms the room's own echo came back through the idle ceiling mics, and gating them fixed it. The reason exists in exactly one place: an email thread in Maya's inbox. Had Noor saved her change, the echo would have returned in 30% of the estate — and nobody would have known why.
items.label: Test: how much of the estate — and where the reason lived.

items.prompt: Where do the reasons behind the architecture live after you've gone?
items.risk: A good decision undone by someone who couldn't find why.
timeout: The reasons stay in one inbox.

hints.text: What would Noor have needed to find, on her own, on Thursday?

Decision records for every key decision — what, why, what else was considered, who owns it — kept with the standard, written with the team, reviewed every year by the standard's owner
options.result: Fourteen records by month seven. Noor writes three. DR-07 is the ceiling-mic gating.
options.consequence: The why travels with the standard.

options.label: A long handover document at the end of your year
options.result: Written in a hurry in month twelve, read once.
options.consequence: The best you can do without documentation habits — late and once.

options.label: Lock the template so nobody can change it
options.result: The next real improvement is blocked too.
options.consequence: Freezes the design instead of explaining it.

items.prompt: So the plan is to teach the juniors everything I know, and then what do you need me for?

options.label: “For the next thing only you can see. Right now you spend every Christmas restoring the platform because nobody else can.”
options.reply: …Every Christmas. Fine. Noor first — she's quick.

options.label: “It's policy.”
options.reply: Policy doesn't restore platforms at Christmas.

options.label: “Nobody's irreplaceable.”
options.reply: Then why am I the only one who can do seven things?

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  To find out what would break if someone left, list every critical task and count who can do it unaided — including yourself — and track that number to zero. Pair each single-person task with a second person signed off by doing it, and credit the expert who teaches. Write a decision record for every key decision — what, why, what else was considered, who owns it — and keep it with the standard. Then prove it: a week without the person you're worried about.
REFLECTION (optional)  · What do you do that nobody else in your team could do next week?
